summary: A short paper about names in data networks. It suggests there are four different kinds of things that can be the destination of a packet, and that the idea of binding, borrowed from operating systems, describes how the four relate.

eli5.summary: Mail can go to a person, a house, or a door, which are different things. This paper points out that networks have similar layers of where a message can be headed.

questions: what are the kinds of network destination names
service vs node vs attachment point
subtitle: A framework for understanding how networks name and locate destinations

tldr.problem: Network designers and researchers discuss names, addresses, and routing in ways that cause confusion, often conflating different concepts or making assumptions about which form of name belongs with which type of object.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes four types of network objects (services, nodes, network attachment points, and paths) and shows how bindings between them explain most network naming and addressing requirements.
tldr.outcome: This conceptual framework helps explain why some network design decisions work well and why certain design choices create subtle problems.

facts.label: Number of binding levels
facts.value: 3 (service to node, node to attachment, attachment to path)

today: RFC 1498 is an informational memo presenting theoretical framework for thinking about network naming and binding. It has not been updated or obsoleted. The concepts remain relevant to modern network architecture and naming systems, providing clear thinking about why certain design choices in DNS, routing, service discovery, and container networking succeed or create subtle problems.

sections.title: The Naming Confusion Problem
sections.content:
Despite efforts to clarify the concepts, discussions about network names, addresses, and routes remain confusing. Some confusion comes from loosely associating network objects with particular forms of names—the assumption that services must have human-readable character string names, nodes must have unique binary identifiers, and attachment points must have hierarchical addresses.

The RFC draws a parallel with operating systems, which faced similar naming challenges with file names, virtual memory addresses, page numbers, and disk block numbers. Operating systems resolved this confusion by introducing the concept of binding: instead of asking 'which form of name goes with which object,' ask 'in what context will a binding for this identifier be found, and to what object is it bound?'

This approach, borrowed from operating system design, provides a systematic framework that applies equally well to data communication networks.
sections.eli5: In operating systems, there are many kinds of names and addresses (file names, memory addresses, disk blocks). Confusion disappears when you think of binding: where is the translation table that explains what this name points to? The same thinking works for network names.

sections.title: Four Types of Network Objects and Three Bindings
sections.content:
The RFC identifies four fundamental types of objects in a data communication network:

Services and Users are the applications (a time-of-day service, an accounting service, a forwarding service) and the clients that use them (a particular workstation or person).

Nodes are computers that can run services or applications. Some are clients; others help implement the network itself.

Network attachment points are the ports where nodes connect to the network—the physical or logical places where a node is 'plugged in.'

Paths run between attachment points, traversing forwarding nodes and communication links.

Most network naming and addressing can be described by three bindings: (1) service to node—which node runs the desired service; (2) node to attachment point—where on the network is that node connected; and (3) attachment point to path—what route leads from here to there.
sections.eli5: To send a message to a service, you need to know: Which computer runs it? Where is that computer plugged in? What path goes from me to that plug? These three questions describe binding at three levels.

sections.title: Permanent and Changeable Bindings
sections.content:
A crucial insight is distinguishing between bindings that change frequently and those that are essentially permanent. When you record that 'the DIALOG service runs on node 5,' three bindings are actually involved, but only one is typically recorded in a changeable table:

The name 'DIALOG Service' is permanently bound to a specific service, management, and data. This binding does not change when you update a table; it would require updating user programs, documentation, and advertising.

The name '5' is assigned to a node on a long-term basis and is not typically expressed in a changeable table.

The binding 'DIALOG is currently running on node 5' is the one typically stored in a lookup table, because we anticipate it might change (the service could move to node 6).

A common design mistake is to believe that updating this table allows you to rename the DIALOG service. It does not; that would require changing the permanent binding, which is stored everywhere except in this particular lookup table. This distinction explains why moving a service is harder than it appears: the table only expresses one of three bindings involved.
sections.eli5: A phone number in a contact list is not the same thing as a person's name. Changing the number does not rename the person. Similarly, in networks, moving where a service runs does not rename the service itself.

sections.title: Real-World Examples and Design Consequences
sections.content:
The RFC illustrates these concepts using real examples. In Ethernet, the 48-bit unique identifier is permanently bound to both the node and the network attachment point. This design choice provides advantages: a node can move to a different physical location without changing network records, the lookup table level is omitted, and a node attached to two Ethernets can use the same identifier on both. But it creates a curiosity: if you want one node to connect to two attachment points on the same Ethernet independently, you must use two different 48-bit identifiers, which might confuse other network records into thinking there are two nodes.

The ARPANET NCP protocol used character-string names like 'RADC-Multics' that appear to be service names but are actually names of network attachment points. This permanent binding of attachment point name created confusion: users expected that the name identified a service that could move. If the Multics computer moved to another ARPANET port, users had to learn a new name, or network administrators had to change tables everywhere. The real issue is that the name is of an attachment point, not of a service bound to a node bound to an attachment point.

Finally, three conceptually distinct binding services (service name resolution, node name location, and route dispensing) are often implemented by a single 'name server,' which may mask the underlying complexity. This merging of services is fine, but understanding the three conceptual bindings helps designers make better choices about what information to store and when.
sections.eli5: Ethernet makes one clever choice: every computer gets one ID that works as both the computer's name and its plug-in point. This simplifies some things but creates odd cases. ARPANET did the opposite: the names are really plug-in points, not computer names. This confused people who thought they were computer names. Understanding which bindings are permanent and which are changeable prevents these confusions.
